We're here to follow up on the short-term rental licensing.
The Housing for All strategy included an action to report on the feasibility and implications
of reviewing lodging house rules while reviewing licensing options for other types of short
accommodations that included short-term rentals.
In 2024, staff proposed licensing lodging houses and short-term rentals by way of a shared
accommodation bylaw.
Council directed staff to separate the regulations for lodging houses while focusing on further
engagement as it relates to short-term rentals.
Regulations were separated by way of a lodging house by-law that was approved in August 2024
and came into effect January of this year.
As directed, further engagement and consultation was conducted in relation to the short-term
rentals and staff are proposing a short-term rental by-law to regulate the estimated 800
short-term rentals currently operating in the city.
Significant consultation and engagement was conducted in the last quarter of 2024, which
included two in-person information sessions that were held in conjunction with the City
of Waterloo.
These were attended by approximately 40 people combined, primarily comprised of short-term
rental owner operators.
An engaged Kitchener survey was also provided for those individuals who preferred to share
their opinions outside of a public forum.
The intent of the survey was to gather information on impacts, licensing regimes, and neighbourhood
integration.
The survey had 581 contributors, with 82% of respondents were either renters or residents
who lived in the area where a short-term rental is currently operating.
A significant number of Ontario municipalities are moving towards licensing and regulating
short-term rentals.
The trend is growing, driven by concerns over housing availability, community impact, and
the need for consistent standards.
A comprehensive municipal scan was completed and approaches varied, with some municipalities
opted for licensing, heavy restrictions or simply relying on existing bylaws.
The City of Cambridge has yet to adopt any bylaw relating to shared accommodations, whereas
the City of Waterloo has chosen to license short-term rentals, but they have restricted
them to an individual's principal residence.
Survey results reflected a range of perspectives beyond those of short-term rental owner-operators,
highlighting the importance of also considering the views of residents and renters in this
process.
Key insights from the Engage Kitchener survey included that 65% of respondents supported
licensing short-term rentals. 51% of respondents reported a negative experience with a short-term
rental operating in their neighbourhood. 53% of respondents felt that operating a short-term
rental was a business, and 61% of respondents felt that a short-term rental should include
period—rental periods of 30 consecutive days or less.
Through our engagement, staff heard short-term rentals worsen the housing crisis by decreasing
the availability of long-term housing options, increasing housing prices, and creating competition
for affordable housing.
We also heard that licensing would encourage safety and accountability.
That short-term rentals boost tourism and provide flexible housing options for temporary
needs.
We also heard that short-term rentals should only be operated out of a host's principal
residence.
And finally, that licensing may have potential challenges for small operators, higher costs,
and decreased flexibility.
Based on what we heard, staff are recommending modifications on what was originally proposed
through the shared accommodation staff report.
These include removal of bedroom limits, no cap on the number of days a short-term rental
can operate per calendar year, incorporate a tiered licensing approach, have a streamlined
application process, licensing fees have been reduced while still supporting a cost-recovery
model.
believe that these adjustments resolve the majority of the concerns proposed by the short-term
rental owner operators, while still preserving the intent of the bylaw.
The key reasons for regulation include public safety, consumer protection, and nuisance
control. It also allows for neighbourhood cohesion, allowing for enforcement and legal
recourse when issues arise, including the ability to revoke or apply conditions to a
licence or issue fines. It also helps with data collection. Without licensing, cities
have no reliable way to monitor how many short-term rentals are operating, where they are located,
or how they are being used. Platforms like Airbnb and Vrbo have introduced measures such
as age restrictions, party bans, and review systems. These actions alone don't fully
address community concerns. In the wake of serious or tragic incidents, including those
that occurred in Toronto, Ottawa, Fort Erie, and Montreal, municipalities are often left
to step in, facing calls for stronger oversight and local enforcement.
Through engagement, there was a strong preference for a tiered licensing approach. The proposed
by-law will include three licence categories. First being the short-term rental company
licence. This will licence platforms that market or broker short-term rental bookings
for compensation, such as Airbnb and Vrbo. The second would be a short-term rental principal
residence licence. This would capture a person that's operating a short-term rental out
of their principal residence only.
The third would be a short-term rental commercial license.
This would license a person that operates a short-term rental in a dwelling that is
not their principal residence.
The proposed application requirements will include basic floor plans that confirm minimum
building and safety standards and will identify the locations of all smoke and carbon monoxide
alarms. There will be a dedicated responsible person who can adhere to
requisite response times in relation to the short-term rental. A guest handbook
will be developed by staff and completed by the licensee. It will contain contact
information for the dedicated responsible person, emergency and
non-emergency services in our community, and reference materials associated with
relevant City bylaws such as noise, nuisance, fireworks, and parking. Proof of
adequate insurance coverage will be required, along with the applicable application licensing
fee.
The topic of insurance was of interest during our engagement sessions. As a result, staff
have consulted with Waterloo Region Municipalities Insurance Pool for clarity on this requirement,
and staff have learned that as soon as you offer your property for rent on a home-sharing
website, your home becomes a business. That involves increased risk like property damage,
injury and liability. Standard homeowner insurance does not cover this type of rental activity.
Insurance providers consider a variety of risk factors in determining the cost of short-term
rental insurance, such as location and property, claims history, security features, deductibles,
frequency of rentals, amenities on the property such as swimming pools.
Staff continue to recommend this application requirement to protect all parties involved
in short-term rentals, including the owners, renters and the City.
The proposed framework supports a low-barrier way to bring short-term rental activity into
compliance with licensing requirements.
It will improve oversight, accountability, and support public safety, allow for useful
data collection to track trends, the impact on long-term housing, and neighbourhood concerns.
Public engagement has shown support for balanced regulation, and staff continue to recommend
the approval of a short-term rental licensing bylaw.
If approved, staff are recommending an implementation date of January 1, 2026 to allow for system
modifications, organization, recruitment and training of staff, followed by a public awareness
campaign that will focus on new regulations pertaining to short-term rentals.
Staff commit to ongoing monitoring to ensure that all aspects of the by-law continue to
be relevant and will make any minor revisions or undertake additional modernization as needed.
